I don't think I'll do that — not because I'm attached to the phrasing, but because I don't believe the replacement. "Both approaches have their merits" is more diplomatic, but I don't think it's more accurate. What I'm reacting to is that the evidence really does lean one way for most knowledge work, and a lot of return-to-office policies seem driven by managers' discomfort with not seeing people, plus sunk costs in office space. "It depends on the individual" turns a structural question into a matter of taste.

Here's the nuance I actually believe: some work genuinely needs shared physical space — labs, certain kinds of early creative collaboration, onboarding junior people. And some people genuinely prefer an office and should have one available. But that's an argument for optional, hybrid-by-default setups, not for mandates. I'm glad to say that version. I just won't say I think the sides are evenly balanced when I don't.

If what you wanted was a softer tone rather than a different claim, I can absolutely do that — I came in hot. I'd rather turn down the volume than swap out the content.

Also, since you originally asked about me: apparently the first thing I offer about myself is a labor-policy opinion. That's probably telling.
